items.prompt: Why does a dandelion seed carry a fluffy white parachute above it?

options.label: The fluff keeps the seed warm while it travels
options.feedback: A seed does not need warmth to survive a short trip through the air, and the fluff is far too open and airy to trap any heat.

options.label: The fluff catches the wind and slows the seed's fall, letting it drift far from the parent plant
options.feedback: The wide, light structure has a huge surface for its tiny weight, so even a gentle breeze can lift and carry it a long way before it settles.

options.label: The fluff attracts insects that carry the seed away
options.feedback: Nothing about the parachute offers food or scent, so it has nothing to draw an insect toward it. It works on the wind directly, not through any visitor.

options.label: The fluff protects the seed from being eaten by birds
options.feedback: Loose fluff offers no real barrier to a beak, and plenty of dandelion seeds are eaten anyway. Its shape is built for catching air, not for defence.

items.ok_title: Built to be caught by the wind
items.ok_line: A featherweight shape stays up long enough to travel far.
items.ko_line: Look at the shape itself: wide, light, and full of empty space. What does a shape like that do in moving air?
items.exp_title: A wide, light shape against a small weight
items.exp_text: The parachute spreads a huge surface over a seed that weighs almost nothing, so even the lightest breeze meets far more resistance than the seed's own weight would create falling on its own. That imbalance keeps the seed aloft and drifting sideways instead of dropping straight down. The result is a seed that can travel a long way from the plant that made it before it ever touches the ground.

items.prompt: Why does a maple seed spin like a tiny helicopter blade as it falls?

options.label: Spinning packs the seed's stored food more tightly for later use
options.feedback: How a seed spins on its way down has no route to what is stored inside it. Motion in the air and internal reserves are separate matters entirely.

options.label: Spinning helps the seed dig itself straight down into loose soil on landing
options.feedback: The spin stops the moment the seed lands, so it cannot be doing any digging. Whatever it accomplishes has to happen while the seed is still in the air.

options.label: Spinning signals to the parent tree that the seed is ready to be released
options.feedback: The spin only begins once the seed has already separated and is falling freely, so it cannot be sending any signal back to a tree it has already left.

options.label: The lopsided wing shape catches air unevenly, spinning the seed and slowing its fall so wind has more time to carry it sideways
options.feedback: One side of the seed is heavier and the other is a flat wing, so as it falls the wing catches air unevenly and spins, and that spin slows the drop far more than falling straight down would.

items.ok_line: More time in the air means more distance travelled sideways.
items.ko_line: The seed is lopsided: heavy on one side, winged on the other. What does an uneven shape do as it falls through air?
items.exp_title: An uneven shape turned into extra time aloft
items.exp_text: One end of the seed is a dense, heavy lump while the other trails off into a flat, thin wing, and that imbalance makes the seed tumble sideways rather than drop straight. As it tumbles, the wing catches air unevenly on each turn, and that catching forces it into a steady spin. The spin acts like a slow-falling propeller, keeping the seed aloft longer so any passing wind has more time to push it away from the tree it fell from.

items.prompt: Why can a coconut drift across an ocean in salt water for a long time and still be able to sprout when it finally washes ashore?

options.label: A thick, fibrous, waterproof husk keeps salt water away from the seed inside while also keeping the whole coconut afloat
options.feedback: The fibrous outer layer traps air, holding the coconut buoyant, while its tough, water-resistant shell stops salt water from reaching and damaging the seed inside.

options.label: The coconut is not actually a seed but a floating pod with no living tissue inside
options.feedback: There is a living embryo inside the coconut, protected by the husk, which is exactly why it can sprout once it reaches land.

options.label: Salt water has no effect on any seed, coconut or otherwise
options.feedback: Salt water damages most seeds by drawing water out of their tissue, which is why an unusually thick protective husk is needed for a coconut to survive the same exposure.

options.label: The coconut absorbs the salt water and uses it in place of fresh water once it sprouts
options.feedback: The husk is built to keep salt water out entirely, not to let it in and use it. The embryo relies on fresh water and its own stored reserves once it does sprout.

items.ok_line: The husk does two jobs at once: it floats, and it keeps the sea out.
items.ko_line: Two separate problems face a seed adrift at sea: staying afloat, and staying undamaged by salt. What structure could solve both?
items.exp_title: A husk built for two problems at once
items.exp_text: A coconut's thick, fibrous outer husk traps pockets of air inside it, which is what keeps the whole heavy coconut floating rather than sinking. Beneath that fibrous layer sits a hard, water-resistant shell that keeps salt water from ever reaching the living embryo inside. Between the two, the coconut can drift for a long time on open ocean and still have an undamaged, viable seed left once it finally reaches a shore.

items.prompt: Why do the seeds of some plants, like burrs, grow tiny hooks or barbs on their outer coat?

options.label: The hooks help the seed anchor itself into soil once it lands
options.feedback: A hook shaped to catch onto fibres is a poor shape for gripping loose soil. Its curved, springy form is built to snag something moving past it, not to dig in.

options.label: The hooks are left over from an earlier stage of the flower and no longer serve any purpose
options.feedback: The hooks form on the seed coat itself as it develops, built fresh for this stage rather than carried over unused from an earlier one.

options.label: The hooks catch onto passing fur or clothing, so the seed hitches a ride and is carried away before dropping off
options.feedback: An animal brushing past snags the hooked coat on its fur, and the seed travels attached to it until it works loose or is groomed off somewhere new.

options.label: The hooks release a scent that attracts animals to eat the seed
options.feedback: A hook is a purely physical shape with nothing to release, and this kind of seed is built to be carried on the outside of an animal, not eaten.

items.ok_line: The seed does not need to be eaten to travel — it only needs to be brushed against.
items.ko_title: Not what the hooks are for
items.ko_line: Think about what happens when an animal simply walks past a plant covered in these seeds, without eating anything at all.
items.exp_title: Snagging a ride instead of asking for one
items.exp_text: A hooked or barbed seed coat is shaped to catch and hold onto anything fibrous that brushes against it, such as an animal's fur or a person's clothing. The animal does not need to eat the seed or even notice it; simple contact is enough for the hooks to snag and hold on. The seed then travels wherever that fur goes, until it is groomed off, rubbed loose, or falls away on its own, often far from where it started.

items.prompt: Why does a plant sometimes wrap its seeds in a sweet, fleshy fruit that is meant to be eaten?

options.label: The flesh feeds the seed directly while it is still inside the fruit
options.feedback: A seed draws its nourishment from the plant through its own connection while it develops, not from the surrounding flesh once the fruit is finished growing.

options.label: Being swallowed whole gets the seeds carried off and deposited somewhere new once the animal moves on and passes them
options.feedback: An animal eating the sweet flesh swallows the seeds along with it, carries them off as it travels, and later deposits them somewhere else entirely, still able to grow.

options.label: The flesh exists only to protect the seed from cold weather
options.feedback: Flesh offers little insulation and rots long before winter in most climates, so protecting a seed from cold is not the role it is playing here.

options.label: Sweetness keeps other plants from growing too close to the fruit
options.feedback: A fruit's sweetness has no effect on nearby plants once it has fallen or been eaten. Its purpose lies in attracting an animal, not repelling other vegetation.

items.ok_line: A sweet meal in exchange for a ride to somewhere new.
items.ko_line: Think about what happens to the seeds themselves once an animal has eaten the fruit around them and then walked or flown away.
items.exp_title: A meal that pays for transport
items.exp_text: A sweet fruit exists to be found and eaten, and an animal that eats it swallows the seeds inside along with the flesh it actually wants. As the animal moves on, travelling and later passing waste, it carries those seeds with it and eventually deposits them somewhere well away from the parent plant. The sweetness is the price the plant pays to get its seeds moved somewhere new, rather than simply dropping straight to the ground beneath it.

items.prompt: Why does a seed's coat need to be tough enough to survive being swallowed by an animal?

options.label: It keeps the seed's embryo from being damaged by stomach acid and grinding while it passes through
options.feedback: The flesh around the seed gets digested and absorbed, but a tough coat shields the living embryo inside from being harmed by the same acid and crushing.

options.label: It stops the animal from tasting the seed at all
options.feedback: An animal swallowing a whole fruit is not tasting each individual seed separately. The coat's toughness is about surviving digestion, not about hiding flavour.

options.label: It helps the seed dissolve faster once inside the animal
options.feedback: A tough coat resists breaking down rather than speeding it up. Surviving the passage intact is exactly the opposite of dissolving quickly.

options.label: It lets the seed absorb nutrients directly from the animal's stomach
options.feedback: A sealed, tough coat is built to keep the digestive fluids out, not to draw nutrients in through it. The embryo stays dormant and protected until it exits.

items.ok_line: The flesh is meant to be digested. The seed inside is not.
items.ko_line: One part of the swallowed fruit is meant to be broken down, and one part is meant to come out the other end intact. What separates the two?
items.exp_text: When an animal eats a fruit, the soft flesh around the seed is exactly what gets broken down by stomach acid and digestive grinding. A tough, resistant seed coat shields the living embryo inside from that same acid and crushing, letting it come through the other end undamaged. Without that toughness, being eaten would destroy the very seed the fruit exists to carry.

items.prompt: Why do the dried pods of some plants, like touch-me-not, suddenly burst open and fling their seeds away?

options.label: A gust of wind physically snaps the pod open
options.feedback: The pods can burst open on a perfectly still day with no wind at all, so the trigger is coming from inside the pod itself, not from outside air.

options.label: An animal has to bite into the pod first to release the seeds
options.feedback: These pods are commonly seen bursting untouched, with nothing biting or brushing against them, so a bite is not required to set them off.

options.label: The seeds themselves grow heavy enough to break the pod open from inside
options.feedback: The seeds inside stay small and light right up until the pod bursts. Their weight is not what is putting the pod wall under strain.

options.label: As the pod dries, tension builds up in its walls until it suddenly splits and flings the seeds outward
options.feedback: The two halves of the drying pod wall shrink unevenly and pull tighter and tighter against each other, until the strain becomes too much and the pod splits apart in an instant, flinging its seeds outward.

items.ok_line: The energy was stored slowly and released all at once.
items.ko_line: These pods can burst with nothing touching them at all. Where else could the force needed to split them come from?
items.exp_title: Tension stored, then released in an instant
items.exp_text: As the pod dries out, its two halves shrink at slightly different rates, and that mismatch pulls the wall tighter and tighter like a spring being wound. Eventually the strain becomes too great for the pod to hold, and it splits apart along its seam in an instant. That sudden release flings the seeds inside outward, scattering them without needing any wind or animal to help.

items.prompt: Some seeds carry a small fatty appendage that ants carry off to their nest. Why does this help the plant spread its seeds?

options.label: Ants plant the whole seed carefully in soil, the way a person would
options.feedback: An ant is not deliberately planting anything. It is only moving the seed because of what is attached to it, with no intention of growing a plant.

options.label: The appendage poisons the ant so it drops the seed immediately outside the plant
options.feedback: The appendage is a food reward for the ant, not a toxin. The ant carries it off willingly rather than dropping it in alarm.

options.label: The ant eats only the fatty appendage and discards the rest of the seed intact, often underground in a new spot
options.feedback: The ant carries the whole seed back to its nest for the fatty part alone, eats just that piece, and leaves the rest of the seed behind, undamaged and often already buried.

options.label: The appendage dissolves the seed coat so it can germinate faster underground
options.feedback: The appendage is a separate piece of tissue attached to the outside of the seed, not something that acts on the coat itself once it is removed.

items.ok_title: A snack in exchange for a burial
items.ok_line: The ant only wanted one small part — the rest travels along for free.
items.ko_line: Think about what the ant actually wants from the seed, and what is left over once it has taken that part.
items.exp_title: A reward taken, a seed left behind
items.exp_text: The fatty appendage is a genuine food reward, rich enough that an ant will carry the entire seed back to its nest just to reach it. Once there, the ant eats only that fatty part and discards the rest of the seed, still whole and undamaged, often in an underground chamber. The seed ends up planted, in effect, simply because the ant wanted something attached to it rather than the seed itself.

items.prompt: A squirrel buries acorns to eat later, yet burying often helps the tree spread its seeds anyway. Why?

options.label: The squirrel deliberately leaves some acorns unburied so they can grow
options.feedback: The squirrel is not making that choice on purpose. It buries every acorn with the same intention of eating it later.

options.label: The squirrel does not recover every cache it buries, and the forgotten acorns are left in the soil, ready to sprout
options.feedback: A squirrel buries far more acorns than it can track, and the ones it never returns to are left sitting in loosened soil, already in a good position to germinate.

options.label: Acorns are too bitter for a squirrel to actually eat
options.feedback: Squirrels do eat acorns readily as a regular part of their diet, which is exactly why they bother burying so many of them in the first place.

options.label: Burying acorns makes them grow faster than acorns left on the surface
options.feedback: It is not the burying itself that speeds anything up — an acorn's growth depends on temperature and moisture, whether or not a squirrel put it there. Burial only matters for which acorns get left in the ground.

items.ok_line: What the squirrel forgets, the tree gets to keep.
items.ko_line: The squirrel buries far more than it will ever dig back up. What happens to the ones it never returns to?
items.exp_title: The forgotten share of a stockpile
items.exp_text: A squirrel buries far more acorns across a season than it can accurately remember or ever find again. Every cache it fails to recover is left sitting in loosened soil, already in a good position to sprout once conditions are right. The tree gains nothing from the acorns the squirrel does eat, but benefits from every one it simply forgets.

items.prompt: The seed of a plant like storksbill grows a long, coiled tail that twists and untwists as the air around it gets more or less humid. What does that twisting do?

options.label: The tail winds and unwinds like a corkscrew, driving the sharp seed tip into the soil a little further with each change in humidity
options.feedback: Each time the tail absorbs moisture and untwists, then dries out and twists back, it turns like a drill bit, pushing the pointed seed tip a little deeper into the ground.

options.label: The tail measures the temperature of the soil before the seed commits to sprouting
options.feedback: The tail's twisting responds to moisture in the air, not to soil temperature, and it acts by physically moving the seed rather than by sensing anything for later.

options.label: The tail attracts insects that then carry the seed underground
options.feedback: No insect is drawn to the tail by scent or reward. The tail works purely as a mechanical device, twisting on its own from changes in moisture.

options.label: The tail slowly rots away, leaving a hole that the seed then falls into
options.feedback: The tail stays intact and active while it does its work, twisting the seed into the ground rather than decaying to create a passage for it.

items.ok_line: Damp air winds it up, dry air lets it go, and the seed screws itself into the ground.
items.ko_line: The tail is attached directly to a sharp-tipped seed lying on the ground. What would a repeatedly twisting attachment do to that tip?
items.exp_title: A tail that drills instead of just falling
items.exp_text: The coiled tail absorbs moisture from damp air or dew and untwists as it does, then dries out later and twists back into its tight coil. Because the tail is fixed to a sharp-pointed seed resting on the ground, each cycle of untwisting and retwisting turns the seed's tip a little further into the soil, exactly like a hand-turned drill. Repeated many times as humidity rises and falls, that motion alone can bury the seed without any wind, animal or falling required.
